1170.title: Praise
1170.hook: hands raised, songs repeated, worship loud and joyful
1170.howItsDone: In Pentecostal and charismatic churches, worship often includes a band, raised hands, repeated choruses and spoken praise; other churches praise through chant, hymns or silence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the love feast: plain bread, water, and testimony. Your line was bread and a story.

The ark of God is coming up into Jerusalem, with shouting and the sound of the trumpet, and the king can't keep still. "And David danced before the LORD with all his might." His wife Michal watches from a window and despises him for it. A king, leaping in the street. David's answer: he'll be lowlier still in his own eyes, before the LORD who chose him. A new week opens with Pentecostal and charismatic Christians, whose worship can look a lot like David in the street.

Step into a Pentecostal or charismatic service and you may find a band, a congregation on its feet, hands in the air, one chorus sung again and again, someone calling out amen, someone in tears, someone very still. From the back row it can look like a concert. To the people there, it's praise: thanking God out loud, with the whole body. Much of it has old roots. Psalm 134 says, "Lift up your hands in the sanctuary, and bless the LORD." Paul's first letter to Timothy pictures people praying everywhere, "lifting up holy hands." Open hands, held up, the way a child reaches for a parent. The repeated songs have old roots too. Psalm 136 gives reason after reason to thank God, and every verse ends with the same answer: "for his mercy endureth for ever." Again and again, until the line isn't something you think about but something you stand on. Hallelujah comes from the psalms as well. Psalm 150 ends, in the King James, "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Praise ye the LORD." That last phrase, in Hebrew, is hallelujah. Christians praise at very different volumes: Orthodox chant, a quiet Anglican evensong, the silence of a Quaker meeting, a Pentecostal church on its feet. The psalms make room for all of them. The same book that says "Be still, and know that I am God" also says, "O clap your hands, all ye people; shout unto God with the voice of triumph."

If you're somewhere you can, lift your hands, palms open, to shoulder height or higher, and hold them there for a few slow breaths; it may feel unusual, and that's all right. Then lower them slowly to your lap, and rest. If you pray, say the psalms' last line, Praise ye the LORD; if you don't, let your open hands be a thank-you for one good thing today.
Praise. Thanking God out loud, with songs, raised hands and the whole body. In Hebrew, hallelujah.
Your line: hands up. Open hands, the way a child reaches. I'll be here tomorrow.

1171.title: Laying on of hands
1171.hook: believers pray with a hand on the shoulder of the one prayed for
1171.howItsDone: In Pentecostal and charismatic churches, people who ask for prayer are often surrounded by others who pray with a hand on their shoulder; Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and other churches ordain ministers with the laying on of hands.

segments.voice: Yesterday, praise: hands raised, songs repeated, David dancing in the street. Your line was hands up.

In Damascus, a disciple named Ananias hears the Lord tell him to go to a house on the street called Straight and ask for a man named Saul. Ananias knows that name. Saul has come to Damascus with authority to arrest people like him, and Ananias says so: he's heard how much evil this man has done. The answer comes back: go. So he walks into the house where Saul sits blind, puts his hands on him, and says, "Brother Saul." Then something like scales falls from Saul's eyes, and he can see.
screen: `A HOUSE ON THE STREET CALLED STRAIGHT.`

segments.voice: Through the New Testament, hands carry prayer. When parents bring children to Jesus, Mark says, "he took them up in his arms, put his hands upon them, and blessed them." Hands that bless. When the church in Antioch sends Barnabas and Saul out, "when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away." Hands that send. On Malta, when the father of Publius lay sick of a fever, Acts says Paul "entered in, and prayed, and laid his hands on him, and healed him." Hands on the sick. James, too, tells the sick to call the elders of the church to pray over them. Pentecostal and charismatic Christians keep this close. When someone asks for prayer, others gather round, and a hand goes on a shoulder or a back while they pray, for healing, for strength, for the Holy Spirit. Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and other churches keep the gesture in their rites, and ordain their ministers with the laying on of hands. In these passages, the hands come with words: a blessing, a prayer, a name. The prayer is to God; the hand says something to the person. Someone is with you, close enough to touch. Now go back to Ananias. The hands on Saul belonged to a man with every reason to be afraid of him. Before Saul could see anything, he felt those hands, and heard himself called brother. It closes the distance between people before it asks God for anything.

If someone you're close to is nearby, ask first whether you may pray for them or hold them in mind, and with a yes, rest a hand lightly on their shoulder; if you're alone, bring someone to mind and rest your own hand over your heart. If you pray, pray for them in your own words, or simply say their name before God. If you don't, hold them with care, gently and briefly.
Laying on of hands. Praying with a hand resting on the person prayed for: to bless, to heal, to send, and to say someone is with you.
Your line: a hand and a prayer. Ananias called him brother first. See you tomorrow.

1172.title: Prophecy and discernment
1172.hook: a word for someone, tested by scripture and the church (1 Corinthians 14:29)
1172.howItsDone: In Pentecostal and charismatic churches, someone may share a word they believe is from God, during worship or privately, and pastors and the congregation weigh it against scripture before anyone acts on it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, laying on of hands: a hand on a shoulder and a prayer said over someone. Your line was a hand and a prayer.

What should a church do when someone stands up and says God has given them a word? In the meetings Paul writes to, one person has a psalm, another a teaching, another a word they say came from God. He doesn't tell them to stop. He gives them an order: "Let the prophets speak two or three, and let the other judge." Speak, then weigh. In Pentecostal and charismatic churches, that pairing is still alive. Someone may stand during worship and say they sense a word for the room, or quietly tell one person something they believe God put on their heart. Then the church listens, and tests it.

In Paul's letter, prophecy isn't fortune-telling. He says what it's for in the same chapter: "he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort." Edification means building up; in the same letter Paul tells the church, "ye are God's building." Build up, urge on, comfort: three jobs. By Paul's measure, a word that only tears someone down has missed its job before anyone checks it. Then comes the weighing. Paul tells another church: "Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Don't sneer at it, and don't swallow it whole. John's first letter says it more sharply: "believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God." In charismatic churches, a word is weighed against scripture by leaders and by the congregation, and the person who gave it is expected to take it humbly if it's set aside. A word doesn't outrank the Bible or the body. Christians read this gift in different ways. Pentecostals and charismatics hold that the gift is still given today, as in the New Testament. Some other Protestants hold that prophecy as new revelation ended with the apostles, and hear Paul's words as being about preaching and teaching scripture. Catholic and Orthodox Christians speak of prophetic gifts in the church, tested by the church's teaching. And Paul's test works on any sentence spoken over someone, at work, at the dinner table, in a text at midnight: does it build up?

Bring one person to mind who could use building up this week, and let a kind word come slowly: not flattery or advice, but something true about them that would hold weight, like a beam in a house. Then test it Paul's way: does it build up, urge on, or comfort? If you pray, hold that person before God while you choose; if you don't, simply hold them with care.
Prophecy and discernment. A word spoken to build others up, and the church's work of weighing it against scripture.
Your line: build up. Speak first, then weigh it with care. That's today, done.

1173.title: Praying for healing
1173.hook: Pentecostals pray boldly for healing, trusting God with the outcome
1173.howItsDone: In Pentecostal churches, the sick are often invited forward during or after a service, and elders or the congregation lay hands on them, sometimes anoint them with oil, and pray aloud for healing; Catholic and Orthodox Christians also practice a sacrament of anointing the sick.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prophecy and discernment: a word spoken, then weighed. Your line was build up.

"Is any sick among you?" That question sits in the letter of James, and the instructions that follow are practical: call the elders of the church, and let them pray over the sick person, anointing with oil in the name of the Lord. In a Pentecostal service, it can be very direct. Near the end, the pastor invites anyone who is ill to come forward. Elders gather. Someone brings a small bottle of oil. Hands rest on shoulders, and the prayers are bold: out loud, by name, asking God to heal this body, this week. Then everyone goes home and lives with whatever happens next.

James goes on: "And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up." Pentecostal churches take that at its word: if the letter says ask, ask out loud. Today's line echoes Isaiah's song of a servant who suffers for others: "he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed." Stripes here are the welts a beating leaves on skin. The New Testament reads this song through Jesus, beaten and crucified, in two directions. Matthew, after Jesus heals a crowd one evening, quotes the verse just before: "Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses." Peter's first letter quotes the stripes line itself, right after saying Christ bore our sins, "that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness." So Christians read it more than one way. Some Pentecostals hold that healing for the body is part of what Christ won on the cross, and pray with that confidence. Other Christians read the stripes first as healing from sin, and see bodily healing as a gift God gives as he wills. Catholic and Orthodox Christians draw on James for a sacrament of anointing the sick. And then there's Paul, with what he called a thorn in the flesh: "For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me." The answer he records: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." Bold asking, and open hands about the answer. Pentecostal prayer for healing tries to hold both.

Bring to mind one person who is ill right now, say their name quietly, and see where they are this minute: a hospital bed, a couch, a waiting room. If you pray, ask God plainly for their healing, by name, the way James's elders did, and leave the outcome in God's hands. If you don't, hold them in mind with care.
Praying for healing. Asking God boldly to heal, as James describes, while trusting God with what comes.
Your line: by his stripes. The welts of a beating, read by Christians as healing. Go gently.

1174.title: Call and response
1174.hook: the preacher calls, the people answer: worship as conversation
1174.howItsDone: In Black church worship, congregations answer the preacher during the sermon with words like amen, well and preach, and the preacher listens and responds to them, so the sermon is shaped by the whole room.

segments.voice: Yesterday, praying for healing: bold asking, and open hands about the answer. Your line was by his stripes.

The preacher is deep into the sermon now, and she isn't talking alone. She says a line, and from the third pew someone answers, "Well!" She says the next one, and from the back, "Preach!" An organ chord fills the gap. She slows down, leans on the pulpit, and asks the room, "Can I get a witness?" The room answers, "Amen!" In the Black church tradition, none of that is an interruption. It's how the sermon gets preached. The preacher calls, the people answer, and worship turns into a conversation.

The shape is in the Bible too. In Nehemiah, the people gather in the street before the Water Gate in Jerusalem to hear Ezra read the law. When he opens the book, he blesses God: "And Ezra blessed the LORD, the great God. And all the people answered, Amen, Amen, with lifting up their hands." A call, and an answer. Amen is the people's word: yes, so be it, this is true. Paul takes it for granted when he writes to Corinth, asking how a listener who can't follow the prayer could "say Amen at thy giving of thanks." In his churches, people answered. Now the word in today's line: witness. A witness, in a courtroom or in the Bible, is someone who tells what they saw. Before he leaves, Jesus tells his followers in Acts, "ye shall be witnesses unto me." So when a preacher asks, "Can I get a witness?" the question underneath is: has anybody else seen this? Is this true in your life too? The amen that comes back isn't applause for the preacher. It's testimony that the word holds. And the conversation runs both ways. A preacher in this tradition listens to the room. When the answers come quick, the sermon builds. When the room goes quiet, the preacher may circle back and say it again, slower, until it lands. The people help carry the sermon. Nobody is just the audience. Every voice in the room has a job, even if the job is one word.
screen: `SAY AMEN AT THY GIVING OF THANKS.`
`A WITNESS SAYS: I SAW IT TOO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a line of scripture you know, or a sentence someone once said to you that turned out to be true. If you agree with it, answer it out loud, as quietly as you like: amen. Then find another true thing, a kindness you received or a lesson learned the hard way, and answer that one too.
Call and response. The preacher calls, the people answer, and the sermon is preached by the whole room.
Your line: can I get a witness? An amen says: I've seen it too. See you tomorrow.

1175.title: The prayer meeting
1175.hook: midweek gatherings where elders pray long, honest, hope-filled prayers
1175.howItsDone: In the Black church tradition, congregations hold midweek prayer meetings where members and elders gather, share needs, and pray aloud for the sick, the struggling and their neighborhood, often alongside hymns and testimony.

segments.voice: Yesterday, call and response: the preacher calls, the room answers. Your line was can I get a witness?

"Peter therefore was kept in prison: but prayer was made without ceasing of the church unto God for him." That's the Book of Acts. King Herod has already had James killed, and now Peter sleeps chained between two soldiers, waiting for morning. Across the city, the church gathers in a house and prays into the night. That room is a prayer meeting. In the Black church tradition, the midweek prayer meeting carries the same spirit: a few chairs pulled close, the faithful who came out on a weeknight, and elders who pray long, honest, hope-filled prayers.

Then the story turns almost funny. An angel wakes Peter, the chains fall off his hands, the iron gate to the city opens by itself, and Peter walks to the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, "where many were gathered together praying." He knocks. A girl named Rhoda comes to the gate, knows his voice, and is so glad that she runs back inside without opening it. They tell her, "Thou art mad." She insists. They say it must be his angel. "But Peter continued knocking." The church had been praying for Peter, and when Peter himself knocked, they argued with the girl at the gate. Scripture tells that on itself, without embarrassment. The midweek prayer meeting has the same honesty. The elders don't polish their prayers. They name the sick, the one who lost a job, a grandson far from home, the light bill, the grief that hasn't lifted. Nothing is too small to say, and nothing too heavy. And the prayers are full of hope, because they remember out loud what God has done before, the times the gate opened. That's the spirit of a saying you may have seen on church signs and kitchen walls: prayer changes things. What does it change? Sometimes the situation; chains fall. Sometimes the people praying, who become the ones who visit, cook, drive, show up. In that room, the prayers ask for both. And notice where it happened: in a house, for a neighbor in trouble.

Hold your street or your building in mind, and name plainly what it's carrying, the way the elders do: someone sick, a family short on money, a house gone quiet since a loss, small needs and heavy ones. Then remember one time something on your street got better. If you pray, bring both before God; if you don't, simply hold your neighbors with hope.
The prayer meeting. People gathered, often on a weeknight, to pray long, honest and hopeful prayers for one another and their neighbors.
Your line: prayer changes things. And Peter kept knocking. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1176.title: Testimony service
1176.hook: church members stand and tell what God has done this week
1176.howItsDone: In Black and Pentecostal churches, a part of the service or a midweek meeting is set aside for testimony: members stand, often beginning by giving honor to God, tell what God has done for them, and the congregation responds aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prayer meeting: honest, hopeful prayers for the people behind each door. Your line was prayer changes things.

A man who lived among the tombs, breaking every chain they put on him and crying out in the hills, is sitting by the lake now, clothed and calm. Mark's Gospel tells it. Jesus has set him free, and as Jesus climbs back into the boat, the man begs to come along. Jesus says no: "Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee." So the man goes home and tells it, all over his region. Not a sermon. A report.
screen: `A MAN BY THE LAKE, CLOTHED AND CALM.`

segments.voice: A psalm sets the pattern: "Come and hear, all ye that fear God, and I will declare what he hath done for my soul." The psalmist doesn't argue. He tells. In Black churches and Pentecostal churches, the testimony service makes room for exactly that. The floor opens, and one after another, people stand and tell what God has done this week. Some begin with a familiar opening, giving honor to God, and then the story comes. A job found. A test result. A son who called after a long silence. A hard week that didn't break them. Sometimes just: I woke up this morning. And the room answers each one, the way it answered the preacher, with amen and thank you, Jesus. At the center you may hear today's line: God has been good. The Book of Revelation gives testimony real weight. It says of the faithful: "they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony." There it's the witness of the faithful under pressure, and some who testify on a Sunday hear their own small reports in that line. Today closes a week of rooms: praise with hands raised, a hand on a shoulder and a prayer, a word weighed, bold prayer for the sick, the preacher calling and the people answering, the prayer meeting naming every need, and now the testimony. In every one, something is said out loud from the pews: a hallelujah, a prayer, a weighed word, an amen, a story.
screen: `I WILL DECLARE WHAT HE HATH DONE.`
`A WEEK OF ROOMS WHERE EVERYONE SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Go back through the week a day at a time, last night, the day before, the start of the week, and look for one good thing: a conversation, a meal, a moment you were helped. When you find it, say it out loud in a sentence or two, plainly, as a report: this happened. If you pray, you can begin it with thanks.
Testimony service. A time in worship when members stand and tell, plainly, what God has done for them this week.
Your line: God has been good. Small reports count too, even I woke up this morning. That's the week.
